narrative:
The year 1493 marks a pivotal moment in the history of global exchange, centered primarily on Christopher Columbus's return from his first voyage to what he believed were islands in the Indian Sea. After encountering fierce storms in February and March that ravaged his ships and pushed the Santa Maria north toward Portugal, Columbus ran into a terrible storm on February 14 that provoked the first of what would become a long series of increasingly febrile religious experiences [[3]]. He finally returned to Europe in March 1493 after a difficult voyage through the Azores that washed him up in Lisbon, where King João II was deeply disconcerted to learn of his discoveries, having previously ignored Columbus as a fantasist [[2]]. On March 15, Columbus wrote to King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella of Spain, announcing that after sailing west from Cadiz he had reached "many islands inhabited by numerous people: in the Indian Sea" [[4]].

Columbus's return voyage had been preceded by troubling encounters with indigenous populations. On January 6, Martin Alonso Pinzon rejoined the expedition bearing a large quantity of gold which he claimed to have obtained by trading, but just four days later, on January 10, Columbus's crews carried off four Indian men and two boys by force at Rio de Gracia or Puerto Blanco [[3]]. The expedition set sail for Spain on January 15, encountering a fair wind [[3]].

The consequences of Columbus's voyage would unfold rapidly and dramatically. Between September 1493 and April 1496, Columbus undertook his second voyage to the Americas with an armada of seventeen ships [[2]]. The biological exchange initiated by these voyages would prove catastrophic: researchers generally agree that human malaria did not exist in the Americas before 1492 [[2]]. By one December 4 following an unnamed landing, thirty-one of the thirty-five colonists who had arrived that day were dead [[1]]. The year 1493 also saw the arrival of the first Africans brought to Jamestown as indentured servants, marking the beginnings of slavery in the United States [[1]].

While these transformative events unfolded in the Atlantic world, elsewhere in 1493 Hosokawa Masamoto seized control of the Kyoto Shogunate in a coup d'état, reshaping Japanese political power [[5]].
